prop: This design was taken against tetel at commit e19a4694bedd1bd2bda91626362f9c2d05f35274; every claim below describes that tree.

Every input the ticket names is present and travels with the memo: prose.jsonl and claims.jsonl ship inside `<memo>.tetel/`, each event in them carries a `timestamp: u64`, the prose→claim citation edges are the `cite` field of prose events, and a rendered ledger claim id is byte-identical to the workspace claim id. Two things the ticket does not name are also true and constrain the design: both loaders discard every timestamp, so the check must read the logs rather than the loaded types; and a prose block's own id is never written into the rendered document, so a residue line naming `P4` names something no reader of the memo alone can locate.

The ticket's anchor — "revised since the last grounding pass" — would have gone silent on the finding the ticket cites. `brief::build` returns every ledger claim unconditionally, including already-grounded ones ("A claim leaves this list only by leaving the ledger itself — never by having been reported on"), so every subsequent pass re-grades a claim whose wording never changed and appends records with strictly later timestamps against the same digest. This is measured, not inferred: in the two shipped memos, tet28's C9 carries ten records on one unchanged digest from three passes spanning 1690 seconds, and tet28's C13 was graded `qualifies` by two passes 918 seconds apart on unchanged text. So an anchor at the *latest* grading advances past any fix-round prose edit as soon as one more pass runs — and the FORK-94 trail the ticket describes ran six rounds. The anchor must instead be the *earliest* record grading the claim's current wording: the moment that wording first entered proof, which a later pass over unchanged text cannot move.

The residue rule is: a prose block is listed iff (a) it is not a heading and carries at least one citation, (b) every id it cites resolves to a claim in the memo's ledger, (c) every one of those claims is in proof under the predicate `analyze_ledger` already uses — some evidence record whose `proposition_digest` matches sha256 of the claim's current proposition, with the empty digest grandfathered — and (d) the timestamp of the event that set the block's current text is strictly greater than the maximum, over its cited claims, of that claim's earliest in-proof record timestamp. Clause (d) settles the ticket's two ambiguities together: the per-claim anchor is the earliest record grading the current wording, and the per-block anchor is the latest of those, so a block is listed only once its whole evidence base has settled and its text has moved since. Run against the two shipped memos it lists nothing: tet28's and tet29's post-grounding prose revisions each accompanied a claim revision, so the new wording's first proof postdates the edit, and tet28's six post-grounding revisions that did not are heading blocks. Given a FORK-94-shaped edit — tet29's P11 moved 600 seconds past the last first proof with no claim touched — it lists exactly that block and nothing else, and giving one of its cited claims a later first proof clears it.

The residue is about any prose whose text postdates the settling of what it cites, not about revision specifically: the block's timestamp is the one that set its current text, whether that was its `Create` or its last `Revise`, both of which carry a `timestamp` on the prose event. Including creations closes an identical exposure at near-zero cost in listings. It is identical because a paragraph written fresh under already-graded claims rests on them exactly as ungradedly as a rewritten one. It is near-zero cost because a paragraph created in a fix round to carry a new assertion normally cites a new claim, and a new claim is not in proof when the paragraph is written; by the time any pass has put it in proof, that first proof postdates the paragraph, so the block never becomes listable. What creation-counting does catch is the case worth catching: a new paragraph written under nothing but old, already-settled claims.

The first-proof anchor makes the line unclearable by anything that did not look at the prose, and that is deliberate: a further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records with later timestamps but cannot move the earliest one, so re-grounding never blesses a listed block. The only two things that clear it are reverting the text, and revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded — which is exactly the remedy the finding calls for, since the defect is prose asserting something no claim carries. The cost, stated rather than hidden: a listing has no cheap discharge, so a flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until the memo's next claim revision, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line. This is a smaller version of a cost this project has already paid badly once — `no scope declared` printed one undischargeable line per claim and buried the findings that were about the document under a constant — but it differs where it matters: this line is about *this* document, never fires on all blocks at once, and names two concrete acts that clear it.

This is the first check to compare timestamps across processes, and the comparison is sound in unit but not in clock. Both sides are produced by a `now_unix` that is byte-identical in the two places it is defined — `SystemTime::now().duration_since(UNIX_EPOCH).map(|d| d.as_secs()).unwrap_or(0)` at evidence.rs:288 and workspace.rs:257, the only two definitions in the worktree — so they are the same unit and epoch, UTC seconds, with no timezone term. What no record establishes is that the two processes kept the same wall clock; `SystemTime::now()` reads the clock of whoever called it. The bound is therefore exact and must be printed rather than implied: an ordering this line reports can be wrong only if the grounding process's clock differed from the authoring workspace's by more than the interval between the prose edit and the pass that first put the cited claims in proof. That interval is the anchor's own doing — first proof rather than last pass puts a whole grounding round between the two events in the case the residue exists for — but nothing in the data bounds it from below, so no claim is made that it is large.

There is no digest-shaped alternative in the sharp sense, and the reason is structural rather than an omission: `out_of_proof` can compare digests because a record carries a digest of the very text it graded, whereas nothing in the record shape names or digests a prose block — not `Subject`, not `Predicate`, not `RecordInput` — and the grounding brief deliberably hands a pass only id, proposition and pin. Giving a record a prose digest would require the grounding pass to read the prose it is supposed to grade blind. A weaker, genuinely clock-free alternative is constructible: have `render --out` append a publication record — per prose block its text digest, per claim its proposition digest and whether anything grades it — so the residue becomes an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock anywhere. It is rejected on resolution, not on cost. A publication log samples state only at the renders the author happens to perform, so a prose edit and the grading that preceded it inside one publication interval are indistinguishable, and the FORK-94 shape — grounding pass, then fix-round prose, then one render — falls entirely inside a single interval and would be missed. The timestamp comparison resolves exactly that ordering, which is why it is worth its stated bound.

prop: The vacuous cases are excluded by the in-proof gate rather than by a special case, and the exclusion is justified by non-overlap: a claim with no records at all is already printed as `ungrounded`, and a claim whose every record grades superseded text is already a machine failure as `out_of_proof`, so a prose block resting on either is already in front of the reader under a line that says something truer about it. Requiring every cited claim to be in proof therefore makes a memo with no evidence ledger, and a memo mid-first-draft, list nothing at all — the residue is empty until a memo has been graded, which is when it starts being able to say anything. Two populations fall outside the rule and are worth naming rather than counting: heading blocks, and paragraphs that cite nothing. A paragraph with no citation is the one place a false assertion can sit with no citation edge to compare against, so its invisibility here is a real gap and belongs in the printed non-coverage list, not in a footnote.

The residue is bullets in the existing flat human-owed list, not a new section, and it is identified by document line as well as by block id. The partition has no sub-headings — it is one list of `  - ` entries, some of which already run to several indented lines, as `mint_windows` and `tree_states` do — so a section would be the only one there and would say by its shape that it outranks the rest. One entry per listed block, plus a single preamble entry carrying what is constant across them: that the ordering rests on two clocks nothing here can prove are the same. Printing that constant once rather than in every bullet follows the precedent this crate set when `no scope declared` was collapsed to one document-level line, on the stated grounds that repeating a constant per row "buried the findings that are about *this* document under a constant". The entry names the block's workspace id and the line in this document where its text begins, because `compose::render` never writes a block's id into the output and an id alone names something a reader holding only the memo cannot find; the offsets come from one new function in `compose`, consumed by `render` so that the block-to-line mapping is described in exactly one place. It also names each cited claim, that claim's first-proof timestamp and the pass that wrote it, and the block's own timestamp — the inputs to the comparison, so a reader can disbelieve the conclusion.

The implementation surface is six declared modification targets and nothing else: one new field on `Findings`; one new function `prose_after_proof` computing the list from the snapshot's `prose.jsonl` and `claims.jsonl` plus the evidence records `check_file` has already loaded; one call to it inside `check_file`'s existing `if snapshot_dir.is_dir()` block, beside `notes_outside_extent` and `mint_windows`, which is where every snapshot-dependent finding is already computed; one `block_offsets` function in `compose` consumed by `render`; one print loop and one added clause in the human-owed scope sentence in `report::render`; and new entries in `NON_COVERAGE`. `machine_check_failed` is not touched, which is what makes this human-owed by construction rather than by intention. Nothing new ships in the snapshot — `prose.jsonl` and `claims.jsonl` are already in `SNAPSHOT_FILES` — no schema changes, no command is executed and no file the document names is opened, so `check`'s standing guarantees are unaffected. Without a snapshot the list is simply not computed, silently, exactly as `notes_outside_extent` and `mint_windows` are not, and the existing missing-snapshot bullet already tells the reader why. Four things belong in `NON_COVERAGE`: false prose that ships alongside a claim revision, which the ticket concedes and this design does not fix; a paragraph that cites nothing, which has no edge to compare against; whether the two clocks behind the ordering agree; and whether the prose is wrong at all, which nothing here judges.

why: The overlap report named F4, which is the fact establishing that prose.jsonl's Create/Revise events carry the timestamps this new function must read and that no loader surfaces them — that is a premise of the claim's "computing the list from the snapshot's prose.jsonl" clause, so it belongs in the citations.

prop: TET-30 is free of the defect that forced both sibling tickets to be reformulated, and free of it for a checkable reason rather than by luck: its trigger reads no English. The citation edge is the `cite` field the author set with `--cites` on a prose event, and the ordering is two integers off two event logs — the rule was executed end to end over tet28's and tet29's shipped logs without inspecting a single character of prose or proposition text. Declaring this design's own modification targets measured a cost of the census mechanism that compounds with each memo the repository accumulates, and it is worth recording where the next ticket in this family will see it. prop: The residue rule is: a prose block is listed iff (a) it is not a heading and carries at least one citation, (b) at least one cited id resolves to a claim in the memo's ledger that is in proof — some evidence record whose `proposition_digest` matches sha256 of that claim's current proposition, the predicate `analyze_ledger` already uses, empty digest grandfathered — and (c) the block's text timestamp is strictly greater than the maximum, over its in-proof cited claims, of that claim's earliest in-proof record timestamp. Both halves of that definition are load-bearing and both were found by attack rather than by design. Keying on text rather than on the last event is what lets a byte-exact revert clear a listing, since prose.jsonl is append-only and a revert can only append a later timestamp. Keying on the citation list as well as the text is what stops a citation-only revision from moving the anchor while the timestamp stays frozen — an unrefused and indeed encouraged act, since `prose::revise` never compares text and its `cite` parameter exists precisely to let an author add a citation to existing prose. Making clause (b) existential rather than universal is what stops a single record-less citation from suppressing a block silently, and it costs nothing, because a claim with no record has no first proof to enter the maximum. The universal in-proof gate was a second actuator: adding one record-less citation suppressed the block with no machine failure. Both are closed by the pair gate and the existential gate, verified in F17 against tet29's real logs, and the untouched memo still lists nothing.

prop: The vacuous cases fall out of the in-proof test rather than needing a special rule, and the test is existential for a reason attack established rather than argument. prop: The implementation surface is six declared modification targets and nothing else: one new field on `Findings`; one new function `prose_after_proof`; one call to it inside `check_file`'s existing `if snapshot_dir.is_dir()` block, beside `notes_outside_extent` and `mint_windows`, which is where every snapshot-dependent finding is already computed; one `block_offsets` function in `compose` consumed by `render`; one print loop and one added clause in the human-owed scope sentence in `report::render`; and new entries in `NON_COVERAGE`. prop: Two digest-shaped alternatives were examined and both fail, though this is not a claim that no third exists. The sharp one — an evidence record carrying a digest of the prose it vouches for, the exact analogue of `out_of_proof` — cannot be built for a structural reason rather than an omission: nothing in the record shape names or digests a prose block, not `Subject`, not `Predicate`, not `RecordInput`, and the grounding brief deliberately hands a pass only id, proposition and pin. Giving a record a prose digest would require the grounding pass to read the prose it exists to grade blind. The weaker one is genuinely constructible: have `render --out` append a publication record — per prose block its text digest, per claim its proposition digest and whether anything grades it — so the residue becomes an ordinal comparison between successive publications with no clock anywhere. It is rejected on resolution, not on cost. prop: Declaring this design's own modification targets took six whole-worktree searches and measured a cost of the census mechanism that compounds with each memo the repository accumulates. A census is a whole-worktree search whose entire output is captured into a fact and shipped in the snapshot; in this repository the previous two memos' snapshots hold whole file dumps on single JSON lines, tet29's longest at 57249 bytes and tet28's at 34477. What such a search costs is a property of an instrument and a moment rather than of the symbol, in two distinct ways. prop: The anchor and the pair gate together make a listing unclearable by anything that did not either restore the settled text or move the evidence. A further grounding pass over unchanged wording appends records with later timestamps but cannot move the earliest one, so re-grounding never blesses a listed block. A citation-only revision cannot silence one either: it changes the citation set, so the block's text timestamp moves to that revision, and pointing a paragraph at a claim already in proof therefore lists it rather than clearing it. Nor can adding a record-less citation, since the in-proof test is existential and an ungrounded claim contributes no first proof. Two things clear a listing. Reverting the text and citations to what they were when the claims settled, which works because the timestamp is looked up by content rather than by event order even though prose.jsonl is append-only. And revising or adding a cited claim and having the new wording graded, which is the remedy the finding calls for, since the defect is prose asserting something no claim carries. The cost, stated rather than hidden: neither remedy is cheap, so a flow-only edit made after a memo's claims have settled stays listed until some claim moves or the edit is undone, and a memo shipped with such an edit ships the line. Nothing in the rule bounds how many blocks that can reach — an author who flow-edits every paragraph of a settled memo will see every paragraph listed, and on a memo like tet29, whose twelve blocks are all cited paragraphs with no headings among them, that is all twelve. So this is not distinguished from the `no scope declared` line that once printed once per claim by being structurally small. It is distinguished by being conditional on what the author did rather than on what tetel is, by being about this document rather than about the tool, and by naming two acts that clear it.
why: Grounding pass k2 refuted the clause "never fires on all blocks at once": tet29's shipped prose is twelve blocks, all cited paragraphs and no headings, so a post-proof flow edit to each lists twelve of twelve, and nothing in the rule structurally prevents that. The distinction from `no scope declared` is that this line is conditional on what the author did, not that a full sweep is impossible. Corrected to the true discriminator.

prop: This residue's trigger interprets no English, which is what separates it from a rule keyed on reading a memo's prose. The citation edge is the `cite` field the author set with `--cites` on a prose event; the heading flag is a boolean on the same event; the ordering is a comparison of integers off two event logs. Text is consumed in exactly two places, both of them byte comparisons and neither an interpretation. The in-proof test feeds a claim's proposition into sha256. And the block's text timestamp is found by testing each event's text and citation list for equality with the current ones, which reads every version of every block's prose as bytes. Nothing anywhere parses a sentence, matches a phrase, or decides what a paragraph is about. What remains undecidable is not the trigger but the verdict: whether a listed paragraph actually asserts something its claims do not carry. That question is not narrowed, hinted at, or scored here. It is handed whole to the reader, which is what putting the line in the human-owed partition means — the partition whose own opening sentence ends "none of this is settled by a passing check".
why: Grounding pass k2 refuted the clause "the one place text is consumed at all is the in-proof digest": C4's own timestamp definition compares a block's text and citation list byte-for-byte against the current ones, which is a second consumption of prose text. Both places are now named, and the point — consumption without interpretation — is unchanged.

prop: The residue rule is: a prose block is listed iff (a) it is not a heading and carries at least one citation, (b) at least one cited id resolves to a claim in the memo's ledger that is in proof — some evidence record whose `proposition_digest` matches sha256 of that claim's current proposition, the predicate `analyze_ledger` already uses, empty digest grandfathered — and (c) the block's text timestamp is strictly greater than the maximum, over its in-proof cited claims, of that claim's earliest in-proof record timestamp. Making clause (b) existential rather than universal is what stops a single record-less citation from suppressing a block silently, and it costs nothing, because a claim with no record has no first proof to enter the maximum. Both shipped memos list nothing as they stand. That includes the one real post-pass prose revision in either of them, tet29's P4 at 1786174635: it is correctly not listed, because it also cites the claim revised in that same fix round, whose new wording only entered proof at 1786175367, and clause (c) takes the maximum. The P11 edit was a construction appended to those logs, which F8 and F17 both record as such and this proposition had blurred into a description of real data. Corrected, and the real datum k3 surfaced — tet29's actual post-pass revision, P4, is correctly not listed — is stated too; F8 already records it.
